analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety rules, penalties, and whistleblower protections for coal miners.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on April 5, 2017 and died there when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen federal mine safety law: it requires independent investigations of major mine disasters, gives the Labor Department power to shut down mines operating under unsafe plans, raises civil fines and criminal penalties for operators who knowingly break safety rules (including up to five years in prison and a $1 million fine for repeat offenders), expands whistleblower protections to every mine employee, and requires underground coal mines to brief miners on hazardous conditions and install atmospheric monitoring systems.
analysis.who_benefits: Miners and their families. The bill gives every mine employee protection from being fired for reporting hazards or refusing dangerous work, guarantees pay when safety orders idle miners, requires operators to brief workers on hazardous conditions before each shift, and puts independent investigators on major mine accidents so families get findings that go beyond the government's own review.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an independent investigation panel, run through the federal health research agency NIOSH, for any accident killing three or more miners, with authority to hold hearings, issue subpoenas, and publish findings [S3].

Extends anti-retaliation protection to all mine employees, protects workers who refuse duties they reasonably believe are dangerous, guarantees immediate reinstatement while a complaint is pending, and bars companies from using arbitration agreements or contracts to waive these rights [S3].

Raises penalties for operators: fines up to $220,000 for specific safety violations like unapproved ventilation changes and skipped rock dusting, double penalties for mines with a pattern of violations, felony charges of up to five years in prison and a $1 million fine for repeat knowing violators, and personal civil and criminal liability for officers and directors who knowingly authorize unsafe conduct [S3].

Requires underground coal mines to brief each miner on hazardous conditions before the miner travels to the work area, and directs the Labor Department to require atmospheric monitoring systems that give real-time methane, oxygen, and carbon monoxide readings [S3].
Guarantees full pay to miners idled by safety withdrawal orders and lets the government close a mine again if the operator refuses to pay workers for idled time [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators — the companies that own and run mines — would bear new compliance costs for monitoring equipment, training, certification, and recordkeeping, plus sharply higher fines and personal criminal exposure for executives who knowingly violate safety rules. Some of those costs could pass to consumers through coal prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mining companies and their executives

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: operators would have to buy and install atmospheric monitoring systems, adopt electronic recordkeeping, pay certification fees for qualified personnel, and raise rock dusting to an 80 percent incombustible-content standard, expenses that fall hardest on small mines and could pressure margins in an already strained coal industry [S3].

The bill raises the criminal bar significantly — felony exposure of up to five years and fines up to $1 million for repeat knowing violations, plus personal liability for corporate officers — which industry has historically argued chills hiring of qualified managers and goes beyond what existing enforcement needed [S3].

Critics of expanded enforcement note that MSHA already inspects every mine multiple times a year and that the 1977 Act had been repeatedly strengthened after disasters, so supporters bore the burden of showing the extra mandates were worth the cost [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits go to a small population — the nation's coal miners — but the stakes for them are life and death, and most of its provisions respond to documented failure modes from past disasters like Upper Big Branch. The costs fall on operators and, indirectly, coal consumers. This is a targeted, well-developed bill whose main weakness is political: it had no Republican support, so it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or markup, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott, the top Democrat on the House Education and the Workforce Committee, introduced the bill on April 5, 2017 with three Democratic cosponsors joining at introduction [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce that same day [S5].
That is the last action ever taken: the committee never scheduled a markup or floor consideration, and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill picked up 20 cosponsors, all Democrats, over the course of the two-year Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators, who avoided new monitoring mandates, higher fines, and executive criminal liability; miners gained nothing from the bill's death.

industries.note: The bill raises fines up to $220,000 for specific violations, doubles penalties for chronic violators, adds felony exposure of five years and $1 million fines for repeat knowing violators, and holds executives personally liable — costs borne entirely by operators and their officers. Miners, the public side of this ledger, benefit directly from the same provisions.

The bill mandates atmospheric monitoring systems in underground coal mines and direct-reading coal dust explosibility monitors, creating demand for manufacturers of that equipment. Safer monitoring serves miners' interests, so the industry gain runs alongside the public's.

The bill's redefinition of 'operator' explicitly includes independent contractors performing services or construction at mines, and requires them to report injuries and man-hours per mine, ending a gap where contract crews sat outside parts of the safety law.
